data.title: Executive Exposure Supports Impersonation
data.summary: Senior staff were extensively documented in public: biographies, photographs, recorded speech, travel and diary detail. That material is what makes an impersonation of them credible — and their authority is what makes the impersonation work.
data.description:
Executive impersonation is the highest-value social engineering attack, and its inputs are almost entirely public. A biography supplies the role and tenure; conference recordings supply enough speech to synthesise a voice; social posts and event listings supply travel, which tells an attacker exactly when the executive will be unreachable for verification.

The attack does not need to be sophisticated. A message from a look-alike domain, sent while the named person is known to be flying, asking a finance contact to expedite something confidential, succeeds on authority and timing rather than on technique.

Personal exposure extends the surface: home addresses in company filings, family members named publicly, and personal accounts with weak protection that are easier to compromise than corporate ones.
data.recommendation:
* Brief executives and their assistants specifically, with the pretexts their exposure supports.
* Agree a verification practice for high-value requests — a call back to a number of record, or a challenge phrase — that applies regardless of who appears to be asking.
* Avoid publishing travel in advance, and delay event posts until after the event.
* Review public filings for personal detail that can be minimised, and protect personal accounts with hardware factors.
data.short_recommendation: Reduce published travel and voice; verify executive requests out of band.
